newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Quick Bulgaria sell-offs boost investors' interest.
newsitem.headline: Quick Bulgaria sell-offs boost investors' interest.

text.p: Crisis sell-offs announced by Bulgaria's socialist cabinet in a bid to raise desperately needed cash have boosted foreign investors' interest but all depends on the pace of economic recovery, investors said on Wednesday.

"Despite the currently grim situation, I am still optimistic about investment here. We have privatisation and green-field investment targets," Global Finance regional chief executive officer Christos Katsanis told Reuters.

In a dash to meet multilateral lenders' requirements to speed up privatisation, along with the closure of loss-making enterprises and banks, the government announced the sale of some 15 major state companies, expected to raise around $1 billion.
"Interest in Bulgaria has grown after the government's latest privatisation offers," a British-Bulgarian Chamber of Commerce official told Reuters.

The companies include the Pirdop Copper Smelter, Alumina aluminium plant, a major polymer producer, chemical companies Orgachim and Agropolichim and the Bourgas and Rousse ship repair yards on the Black Sea and the Danube river ports, respectively.
Six big foreign investors are vying for a 60 percent stake in Sodi Devnya, the biggest producer of calcined soda in the region, a privatisation agency official said.

South Korea's LG Group, U.S. firm Rhone-Poulenc Rorer Inc, Belgium's Solvay & Cie and Brunner Mond Plc have shown interest in the chemical group, bids for which are accepted until October 10, the agency said.

The murder of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov, millionaire, businessman and parliamentarian for the ruling Socialists, is another sign of the country's instability, one resident foreign businessman said.

Investors are also watching the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Washington for word on whether Bulgaria has won a delayed second tranche of an IMF loan, crucial to haul the country out of economic crisis.

Sofia, grappling with bank insolvency and the collapse of the lev, which plunged from 70 to the dollar in January to about 230 this week, has effectively closed nine banks by putting them under state supervision and hiked the central bank interest rate to an all-time high of 300 percent.
The rate rise and Sofia's decision to speed up privatisation, were designed to convince the IMF to release the promised $115 million tranche and restore confidence in the ailing economy.

Local analysts, however, expected the effect of the rate rise to be shortlived as the burden of internal debt payments would become unaffordable. Yields on government treasury paper have risen as high as 450 percent for individual investors.
Western diplomats said they thought the measures would convince the IMF to release the funds.

But Bulgaria's industry ministry has still not disclosed progress on pledges to close 64 loss-making state enterprises, raising doubts among local economists whether the Fund will approve Bulgaria's sluggish reform performance.
One banker predicted a new wave of bank closures as drastic measures by the central bank were too little, too late and could not compensate for the problems of some banks left open.
Foreign banks have expressed interest in whether stakes in the effectively closed banks will be offered at lower prices, one central bank official, who declined to be named, said.

The South Korean concern Daewoo DWGR.CN had shown interest in Balkanbank, Greek companies were interested in the Bank for Agricultural Credit and Bulgaria's state-owned Bulbank was in talks over acquisition of the ailing Economic Bank.
"Everything depends on how will the business environment develop and what guarantees for investors the country will provide, regardless of government changes," said Katsanis.

Plagued by rising prices, a battered economy and uncertain prospects, Bulgarians have withdrawn support for the cabinet, which came to power in January 1995. Opinion polls suggest 67 percent consider Prime Minister Zhan Videnov inept in dealing with the economic crisis.
